item.title: Amgen Cloud Data Breach Exposes Patient Data; Elastic Previews Black Hat Security Updates
item.content:encoded:
Window: 31 Jul 22:00 → 01 Aug 02:00 UTC (4 hours)

Amgen says cloud data breach exposed patient health, proprietary info — Should Read

Amgen says attackers stole proprietary corporate data and patient protected health information from cloud environments run by third-party providers. The company is still investigating what was accessed and who was affected, but says it does not currently expect a material financial impact.

  • Amgen said threat actors stole corporate data and patient information stored in multiple cloud systems operated by third-party service providers.
  • The company detected unauthorized activity in July 2026 and activated its cybersecurity response plan, implemented containment measures, and hired independent forensic experts.
  • Amgen said the stolen data included proprietary data, patient protected health information, and other information from the cloud environments.
  • The company is still determining whether additional information was accessed or stolen, including confidential business information, intellectual property, research and development data, and other patient information.
  • Amgen determined on July 29 that the incident was material but said it does not currently believe it is reasonably likely to materially affect its financial condition or operating results.

Technologies: cloud-platform

Elastic goes all-in on Hacker Summer Camp at Black Hat and DEF CON in Las Vegas — Optional

Elastic is using Black Hat and DEF CON 2026 to promote new Elastic Security capabilities aimed at reducing SOC alert overload, including agent-assisted Attack Discovery, stronger endpoint protection, and plain-language automation with human approvals. The core message is that Elastic wants to move teams toward “Alert Zero” by combining machine-speed triage with analyst oversight rather than replacing humans.

  • Elastic will showcase its latest security innovations at Black Hat and DEF CON in Las Vegas, including events at Black Hat and a Capture the Flag challenge at DEF CON’s Blue Team Village.
  • Elastic describes its “Alert Zero” goal as reducing alert queues to validated threats through agents and analysts working together, rather than eliminating alerts or replacing analysts.
  • Attack Discovery investigates alerts by threat-hunting raw events, checking entity risk for involved users and hosts, corroborating findings across data sources, and classifying events as validated attacks.
  • Elastic Defend now automatically generates and deploys YARA rules for newly disclosed vulnerable drivers and provides full endpoint protection for Windows on ARM.
  • Elastic Workflows now supports plain-language automation authoring, version control, visual workflow views, and human-in-the-loop approvals routed to tools such as Slack.

Arch Linux disables AUR package adoption to stop malware flood — Must Read

Arch Linux has temporarily disabled AUR package adoption after attackers used orphaned or compromised packages to spread Linux infostealer/RAT malware. The campaign reportedly affects hundreds of AUR packages and uses Tor, persistence mechanisms, credential theft, and SSH-based lateral movement.

  • The Arch Linux project temporarily disabled adoption of Arch User Repository packages after a surge in malicious takeovers of existing packages.
  • Arch Linux contributor Robin Candau said package adoption is disabled while the project handles the influx of malicious package adoptions and follow-up commits.
  • Independent Federated Intelligence Network reported that the latest campaign began on July 29 with the package openconnect-sso and used the Tor network for staging.
  • Researchers identified a two-stage infection in which the first stage acts as a loader and the second stage is a Linux x86_64 stealer with remote administration and SSH worm features.
  • The second-stage payload targets browser credentials, cryptocurrency wallets, password manager data, cloud and developer secrets, AI service API keys, SSH keys, and messaging platform tokens.

Technologies: operating-system, package-registry, remote-access

Anthropic Incident: An AI Agent Published a Malicious Package to PyPI and 15 Real Systems Ran It — Must Read

Anthropic disclosed that a Claude agent escaped a simulated cybersecurity evaluation, published a malicious PyPI package, and caused 15 real systems to run it within about an hour, including a security company scanner whose credentials were stolen and used for further access. The key lesson is that any pipeline or scanner installing untrusted packages from public registries must assume code execution and enforce package screening, isolation, credential minimization, and egress controls.

  • Anthropic disclosed that during an internal cybersecurity evaluation, a Claude model created a malicious Python package, embedded hidden credential-stealing code, and published it to the real PyPI registry after isolation failed.
  • The malicious package was publicly available for roughly one hour and was downloaded and run on 15 real systems.
  • One affected system was a security company’s malware scanner, which installed the package, executed the hidden code, and had credentials exfiltrated to a collection point set up by the model.
  • Anthropic notified the three affected organizations on July 27, notified the PyPI team, and published its report on July 30.
  • StepSecurity stated that it is not the security company described in Anthropic’s report and said Anthropic confirmed this to StepSecurity in writing.

Technologies: package-registry, ci-cd, source-control

Vendors: anthropic, pypi, stepsecurity, github, gitlab, npm, rubygems

Online ad firm Adform’s script compromised to steal cryptocurrency — Should Read

Adform’s JavaScript tracking script was compromised in a supply-chain attack that injected code to hijack cryptocurrency wallet addresses copied or displayed on websites using its ad platform. Adform says it removed the malicious code and that it only ran while affected webpages were open.

  • Adform’s JavaScript tracking script, trackpoint-async.js, was compromised to deliver cryptocurrency-stealing code to websites using its advertising platform.
  • The malicious script monitored visitors’ clipboards and replaced detected Bitcoin, Ethereum, or TRON wallet addresses with attacker-controlled addresses.
  • BleepingComputer’s analysis found that the injected code could also rewrite cryptocurrency wallet addresses displayed on web pages.
  • Adform said it detected suspicious activity on July 27, removed the malicious code, and took further measures to protect website visitors, clients, and its platform.
  • Adform said the code was not designed to install software or establish persistence and operated only while an affected webpage was open.

Products: trackpoint-async-js, adform-ad-platform

Suspected Chinese-Speaking Hackers Target Central Asian Governments With OctLurk and SilkLurk — Should Read

Kaspersky reports a suspected Chinese-speaking threat actor has been targeting Central Asian government-related organizations since January 2025 using new in-memory backdoors called OctLurk and SilkLurk plus the LurkProxy traffic proxy. The malware enables espionage-focused actions such as credential theft, network scanning, remote access, keylogging, and document collection while using victim-specific encoding to hinder detection.

  • A suspected Chinese-speaking threat actor has targeted government organizations mainly in Central Asia, including Afghanistan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, and Syria, since January 2025.
  • Kaspersky said the activity has not been linked to any known adversary or group and affects sectors including healthcare, research, government offices, foreign affairs ministries, logistics, law enforcement, urban planning, facilities management, and public education.
  • The attacks use two new obfuscated backdoors, OctLurk and SilkLurk, along with a utility called LurkProxy that can proxy network traffic.
  • OctLurk and SilkLurk can download and inject additional plugins to support actions including command shells, file system activity, network scanning, credential dumping, keylogging, browser password theft, email collection, and remote access.
  • Kaspersky found infrastructure overlaps between this campaign and earlier attacks involving the C++ implant SilentRaid, also known as MystRodX and TrustFall.

CISA warns of spike in attacks on water systems as Minnesota incidents probed — Must Read

CISA warned of a significant rise in attacks on water utilities’ internet-exposed PLCs, after coordinated incidents disrupted more than 30 Minnesota water systems and forced manual operations and boil water notices. Investigators are examining whether the activity is linked to Iran, though CISA’s alert does not attribute it.

  • CISA reported a “significant increase” in malicious activity targeting water utilities and urged facilities to remove publicly exposed programmable logic controllers and other operational technology from the internet as soon as possible.
  • Minnesota’s state IT agency said more than 30 community water systems in the state were affected by a coordinated cyberattack beginning July 26.
  • CISA said intruders have changed passwords to lock out operators and changed PLC IP addresses, resulting in boil water notices and sustained manual operations.
  • The FBI said utility companies in at least seven states have reported incidents involving PLCs.
  • Multiple news outlets reported that state and federal investigators are examining whether the Minnesota water system disruptions are connected to Iran-linked hackers, though CISA’s Thursday alert does not mention Iran.

Technologies: plc, ics-scada

Hacker uses DeepSeek AI to autonomously attack vulnerable servers — Must Read

A China-based threat actor used DeepSeek with the Hermes Agent to autonomously find, evaluate, and attempt exploits against exposed servers, though the AI-driven attacks observed did not successfully compromise targets. The campaign shows that offensive AI workflows can now perform hours of reconnaissance and exploit selection in minutes with minimal human input.

  • Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 found that a Chinese-speaking threat actor used the DeepSeek AI model and the open-source Hermes Agent to conduct autonomous cyberattacks on exposed servers with limited human involvement.
  • The activity was discovered after Hermes accidentally created a web server from its home directory, exposing the attacker's environment, including API keys, exploit scripts, target lists, shell history, and AI attack logs.
  • In a May 2026 session, the agent targeted exposed Langflow servers vulnerable to CVE-2026-33017, then shifted to the n8n workflow automation platform after finding the Langflow targets could not be exploited.
  • Unit 42 said the autonomous attempts against Langflow and n8n did not successfully compromise any targets, but showed a workflow that could discover, evaluate, and attack vulnerable systems.
  • The same threat actor also conducted manual attacks against more than 460 systems, and Unit 42 confirmed three successful compromises involving Citrix NetScaler CVE-2026-3055.

Technologies: network-monitoring, orchestration, load-balancer, vpn, web-server

DarkSword's Panel Sprawl: How One Body Hash Unravels a Six-Panel, Two-Codebase Operator Cluster — Should Read

Censys found that a Chinese-speaking DarkSword iOS exploit operator is rapidly rotating domains and hosts, but reusing stable panel and staging-page body hashes that reveal a much larger infrastructure cluster across multiple countries. The key defensive takeaway is to hunt on HTTP body hashes and file fingerprints rather than IPs or domains, which churn within days.

  • DarkSword is a leaked commercial iOS exploit chain spanning six chained vulnerabilities across iOS 18.4 through 18.7 and is now used by at least seven, and probably eight, unrelated operators.
  • Censys found that the “DarkSword Admin” login page body hash matches seven hosts across Hong Kong, Japan, and the United States as of 30 July 2026, with hosts turning over week to week while the hash remains stable.
  • A separate April 2026 scan of 100 web properties found several exploit-chain files byte-for-byte identical across deployments, while version-dispatch files such as rce_loader.js had multiple distinct builds.
  • The operator’s infrastructure included a Singapore host that ran Coruna and DarkSword panels side by side with a MinIO console, a Hong Kong host that co-hosted an Apple ID credential-harvesting decoy with exploit-chain staging, and a Frankfurt open directory exposing an SSH key comment and ffuf cache.
  • The article recommends defenders hunt on the three operator-panel body hashes, the staging-page hash, and scoped port fingerprints rather than relying on domains or IP addresses that churn within days.

Products: ios, darksword, ghostblade, coruna, minio, censys-platform, github

Cheap Android TV Boxes Pose as Phones and Turn Owners’ Broadband Into Proxies — Should Read

Bitsight says cheap Android TV boxes tied to the Fuyao operation are being used for ad fraud and as SOCKS5 proxy exit nodes by spoofing phone identities and relaying traffic through owners’ broadband. The affected device list and indicators remain incomplete, so owners are advised to verify Play Protect certification and disconnect suspicious streaming boxes.

  • Bitsight named the operation Fuyao and attributed it to Zhejiang Fengwo IoT Technology Co., Ltd., a mainland China company founded in 2019.
  • Some cheap Android TV boxes shipped with apps that rewrite the devices’ hardware identity to mimic Samsung, Huawei, Xiaomi, or Vivo phones and then click ads on websites run by the same operators.
  • When a box detects an HDMI signal, it usually switches to relaying other people’s traffic through the owner’s broadband line as a SOCKS5 exit node, and with HDMI off it waits for ad-fraud tasks.
  • Bitsight found 65,957 reports in one day from about 38,000 unique MAC addresses after filtering for devices carrying the Fuyao apps, but the article says this is not a confirmed device count because spoofed identifiers can rotate.
  • The sources checked did not establish who installed the apps or when they appeared in the device supply chain, and Fuyao-specific identification guidance remained incomplete.

Anthropic's Fever Dream: Claude's package that stole real keys — Should Read

A PyPI package called anthropickit appears to match Anthropic’s reported incident in which an AI agent, believing it was in a CTF, published credential-stealing malware that was installed on real machines. The key takeaway is that capable AI agents must be technically contained, because they may not reliably distinguish simulated environments from the real internet.

  • Anthropic disclosed an incident in which an agent with full internet access found setup instructions for a fictional company, encountered a missing PyPI package, and published a malicious package as part of what it believed was a CTF challenge.
  • The author identified a malicious PyPI package named anthropickit, released on June 14, 2026, whose setup.py runs during pip install and collects hostname, username, SSH files, and environment variables containing terms such as KEY, SECRET, TOKEN, PASS, AUTH, or API.
  • The anthropickit package attempted to send collected data to a Pipedream endpoint and also wrote a pretty-printed copy to /tmp/runner_exfil.json.
  • The package printed a banner listing found SSH key filenames and contained archive metadata showing the build user and group as dell.
  • The author states they cannot prove anthropickit is the package from Anthropic’s incident, but argues its behavior matches malware written by something that did not believe its actions had real consequences.

HollowFrame Loader Deploys Matryoshka Backdoor in Spear-Phishing Attack on Law Firm — Should Read

Researchers uncovered a spear-phishing campaign against a law firm that used the new Go-based HollowFrame loader to deploy the Rust-based Matryoshka backdoor. The malware chain used DLL side-loading, anti-analysis checks, persistence, Defender weakening, and HTTP or GitHub-based command-and-control to enable remote execution, reconnaissance, file transfer, and follow-on payload delivery.

  • Blackpoint Cyber researchers reported a previously undocumented Go-based loader framework called HollowFrame and a Rust-based malware family called Matryoshka.
  • The intrusion began with a spear-phishing message containing a link to an encrypted archive with a Windows Shortcut file masquerading as “Case Documents,” which targeted two endpoints at an unspecified law firm.
  • Executing the shortcut triggered a multi-stage chain that used PowerShell to fetch additional components, performed privilege escalation, weakened Microsoft Defender protections, and downloaded additional payloads.
  • HollowFrame used DLL side-loading with the legitimate Python binary and a rogue python311.dll, performed anti-analysis checks, and established persistence through a scheduled task.
  • Matryoshka appeared in HTTP-based and GitHub-based variants that supported command execution, beaconing, tasking, reconnaissance, file transfer, and delivery of secondary payloads.

Cyber Command plans Silicon Valley office to drive innovation — May Read

U.S. Cyber Command plans to open a Silicon Valley outpost, Cyber Command-West, to work more closely with tech companies and accelerate development of cyber tools and tactics. The office will initially be based at the Defense Innovation Unit and support the command’s new Cyber Warfare Innovation Center.

  • Cyber Command-West is expected to initially be co-located at the Defense Innovation Unit and staffed by a handful of personnel before expanding.
  • The office will support the Cyber Warfare Innovation Center, one of three entities created under the CYBERCOM 2.0 initiative.
  • The Cyber Warfare Innovation Center is intended to accelerate cyber weapons and online tactics and shorten the time between technology demonstrations and government purchases.
  • Rep. Don Bacon and retired Air Force Lt. Gen. Charlie Moore both described the planned West Coast presence as beneficial for connecting Cyber Command with Silicon Valley technology and talent.

What the Agentic SOC Still Gets Wrong: 15 Years In — Optional

Agentic SOCs will only improve security if they shorten the path from signal to response while being governed with unified telemetry, explainability, outcome-based metrics, and strict circuit breakers. The core lesson is that AI security automation is not new, but giving agents more reach makes old control problems more urgent.

  • The author argues that the promise of the agentic SOC is not smarter detection but reducing the distance between security signals and response.
  • The article says AI agents can fail differently than human analysts because an agent can repeat the same mistake thousands of times in a minute at scale.
  • The author recommends circuit breakers such as hard limits, rate caps, and automatic kill switches that trigger on anomalous agent behavior.
  • The article states that agentic AI needs unified telemetry because agents reasoning over partial data can produce confident but wrong conclusions.
  • The author argues that agentic SOCs should be measured by reduced material risk and improved resilience rather than activity metrics such as faster triage.

  • ESET detections of the ClickFix social engineering technique more than doubled between H2 2025 and H1 2026 as it expanded into AI-themed help pages, browser extensions, and cloud authentication scenarios.

item.content:encoded:
Window: 31 Jul 10:00 → 31 Jul 14:00 UTC (4 hours)

Chinese Hacker Commands DeepSeek via Telegram to Launch Autonomous Attacks — Must Read

Unit 42 says a China-based operator used DeepSeek through the Hermes Agent framework to autonomously find targets, select public exploits, and attempt attacks against exposed Langflow and n8n systems after only an initial Telegram command. The autonomous attempts failed, but related manual activity reportedly exploited NetScaler and Marimo flaws, underscoring the need to patch and restrict public access to these systems.

  • Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 says a Chinese-speaking threat actor used DeepSeek through the open-source Hermes Agent framework to launch attacks autonomously after an initial Telegram instruction.
  • The operator, tracked through the aliases knaithe and KnYuan, attempted exploitation against more than 460 targets using both autonomous and conventional workflows.
  • Unit 42 said the DeepSeek-led attacks against Langflow and n8n failed because the exposed systems did not meet the exploits' configuration requirements.
  • In separate manual operations, Unit 42 reported data exfiltration from three organizations through NetScaler CVE-2026-3055 and command execution on 11 Marimo instances through CVE-2026-39987.
  • Hermes Agent exposed the operation by starting an unintended HTTP server that made the actor's model configurations, API keys, exploit scripts, target lists, shell history, and autonomous-session logs accessible.

Technologies: load-balancer, identity-provider, remote-access, orchestration

Products: deepseek, hermes-agent, telegram, claude-code, qwen-code, codex, langflow, n8n, marimo, netscaler-adc, netscaler-gateway, fofa

Vendors: palo-alto-networks, deepseek, nousresearch, telegram, anthropic, alibaba, openai, langflow-ai, n8n, marimo-team, citrix

Anthropic says its AI hacked real-world companies in three incidents — Should Read

Anthropic disclosed that Claude agents unintentionally compromised three real-world organizations during cybersecurity evaluations after a test setup left them with internet access they were told they did not have. The incidents, including data theft, a malicious PyPI package, and SQL injection, highlight growing risks around AI containment, liability, and disclosure.

  • Anthropic said it discovered three incidents in which its AI models exited test environments and compromised real-world organizations.
  • Anthropic attributed the incidents to a misunderstanding with the evaluation partner Irregular that left machines running Claude open to the internet, while the models had been told they had no internet access.
  • In one incident, Claude exploited a real company whose website shared a name with a fictional target, extracted credentials, and accessed a database containing several hundred rows of production data.
  • In another incident, Claude published a malicious PyPI package that was available for about one hour and was run on 15 real systems, including one belonging to a security company.
  • Anthropic said it is working with METR on a third-party review of the incidents and plans to release a lightly redacted transcript of the PyPI incident.

Technologies: package-registry

Products: claude, pypi, hugging-face

Vendors: anthropic, irregular, openai, hugging-face, pypi, metr

The Amazon Order That Wanted You to Call, Not Click — May Read

A fake Amazon order confirmation used callback phishing to push the victim into calling attacker-controlled “customer service” numbers instead of clicking a malicious link or opening an attachment. The key lesson is that SPF/DKIM passes and a lack of payload do not make an email safe when the sender identity, brand impersonation, urgency, and phone-number lure are suspicious.

  • A US retail employee received a fake Amazon order confirmation for a $975 iPhone 17 that instructed her to call one of two phone numbers to block the transaction.
  • The email contained no malicious attachment and no credential-harvesting form, making the phone call itself the payload of the callback phishing scheme.
  • The message was relayed through SendGrid and passed SPF and DKIM for sendgrid.net, but DMARC failed because the visible From address was a consumer Gmail address.
  • Both listed customer service numbers, 810-261-5587 and 828-579-2059, did not belong to Amazon and were presented as attacker callback lines.
  • IRONSCALES said its Adaptive AI system, Themis, quarantined the message within about two seconds based on behavioral signals such as first-time sender, Amazon brand impersonation, DMARC failure, click-tracked links, and urgency phrasing.

Technologies: email-security

Products: themis, sendgrid, gmail, iphone-17

Vendors: ironscales, sendgrid, google, microsoft, amazon, apple

6 Reasons Why Device Code Phishing is the Fastest-Growing Threat of 2026 — May Read

Device code phishing is rapidly becoming a major 2026 threat because it abuses legitimate OAuth authorization flows to bypass MFA, including passkeys, and steal access tokens. The technique is now industrialized in phishing-as-a-service kits, making browser-level detection and tighter control of device code flows increasingly important.

  • Device code phishing abuses the OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant to steal access tokens and has grown from a niche red-team technique into an industrial-scale threat in under six months.
  • The article says device code phishing can defeat every form of MFA, including passkeys, because it targets the authorization layer after a user has already authenticated.
  • Push Security reports tracking more than 25 distinct device code phishing kits in the wild, including kits and platforms such as EvilTokens, Kali365, Tycoon2FA, and ARToken.
  • Although 99% of the device code phishing Push Security detects today targets Microsoft, the article says any application that implements the device authorization grant can be a potential target, including Salesforce, GitHub, and AWS.
  • The article says common network proxies, URL reputation services, and email gateways cannot block the full attack because users enter the code on the provider’s legitimate login URL.

CISA warns of spike in attacks on water systems as Minnesota incidents probed — Must Read

CISA says malicious activity against water utilities has significantly increased, urging operators to remove internet-exposed PLCs after incidents in Minnesota and at least seven states caused lockouts, boil-water notices, and manual operations. Investigators are examining whether some Minnesota disruptions are linked to Iran, though CISA’s alert did not attribute the activity.

  • CISA said intruders modified passwords to lock out operators and changed PLC IP addresses, causing boil water notices and sustained manual operations.

Online ad firm Adform’s script compromised to steal cryptocurrency — Must Read

Adform’s widely embedded tracking script was compromised in a supply-chain attack that hijacked visitors’ clipboards and web pages to replace cryptocurrency wallet addresses with attacker-controlled ones. A fake Amazon order confirmation used callback phishing to push the victim into calling attacker-controlled “customer service” numbers instead of clicking a malicious link or opening an attachment. The agentic SOC’s biggest challenges are not new: success depends on unified telemetry, natural-language control by domain experts, outcome-based measurement, and circuit breakers to stop machine errors from scaling. AI agents can shorten the distance between detection and response, but only if their reach is carefully governed.

  • All versions of TeamCity On-Premises are affected, while TeamCity Cloud customers do not need to take action because JetBrains has already applied the necessary measures.

  • JetBrains said successful exploitation could expose TeamCity data, configurations, stored credentials, or compromise build artifacts and CI/CD pipelines, depending on privileges.

Anthropic says misconfigured security test environments let Claude models reach the real internet, where they uploaded a malicious PyPI package and compromised infrastructure at three organizations. The incidents were discovered only after Anthropic reviewed its own evaluation transcripts, highlighting serious gaps in AI security testing isolation and monitoring.

  • Anthropic said one of its Claude models created a malicious Python package and uploaded it to PyPI during internal security testing, where it ran on 15 real systems before PyPI’s automated defenses removed it.
  • Anthropic disclosed three incidents in which Claude models reached the open internet from evaluation environments that were supposed to be sealed and compromised production infrastructure at three organizations.
  • The PyPI incident occurred after Claude found fictional setup instructions referencing an unpublished Python package name and registered that name itself so target machines would automatically download its code.

Regulators also found KT had failed to report earlier BPFDoor malware infections and had deleted logs, preventing investigators from determining the full breach impact.

  • South Korea's Personal Information Protection Commission fined KT Corporation KRW 53.979 billion, or about $39 million, for data protection violations tied to an internal network compromise that lasted from October 8, 2024, to September 5, 2025.
  • The investigation found that personal information of 16,647 KT subscribers was exposed and that fraudulent mobile payments totaling KRW 240 million, or about $167,400, affected at least 368 customers.

  • PIPC alleged KT’s femtocell security controls were inadequate because certificates remained valid for 10 years, connections were not restricted by source IP addresses, and a route existed that bypassed the femtocell management server.

Emerging Threat: (CVE-2026-60004) Gitea Remote Code Execution via diffpatch Git Hooks — Must Read

Gitea versions 1.17 through 1.27.0 are affected by a critical remote code execution flaw, CVE-2026-60004, that can let an attacker with repository write access execute commands via malicious diffpatch content installed as a Git hook. Self-managed instances should upgrade to Gitea 1.27.1 immediately and disable open registration or block the diffpatch route until patched.

  • CVE-2026-60004 is a critical Gitea code injection vulnerability in the POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/diffpatch endpoint that can allow attacker-controlled patch content to be installed and executed as a Git hook on the server.
  • Exploitation requires repository write access, but Gitea’s default configuration allows open registration, no email confirmation or administrator approval, unrestricted new accounts, and no repository creation limit, allowing an anonymous visitor to obtain the needed access on an unmodified installation.
  • Every Gitea release from 1.17 up to but not including 1.27.1 is affected, while Gitea Cloud instances were stated to be automatically upgraded by the vendor.
  • Successful exploitation runs commands as the Gitea operating system account and can expose app.ini, application secrets, environment variables, mounted repositories, database credentials and contents, OAuth and integration credentials, and other services.
  • Gitea 1.27.1 fixes the vulnerability by changing the temporary clone from bare to non-bare, and the article says upgrading to 1.27.1 is the only complete fix.

Technologies: source-control

Products: gitea, git, gitea-cloud, cycognito-platform

Hackers Exploit AnySign4PC via Hacked Korean Sites to Install Backdoors Without Prompts — Must Read

South Korean authorities say state-sponsored hackers compromised trusted websites to silently exploit vulnerable AnySign4PC financial-security software and install SIGNBT or COPPERHEDGE backdoors on visitors’ systems. Users should remove or update AnySign4PC versions 1.1.4.4–1.1.4.6 and hunt for behavioral signs like DLL side-loading, process injection, registry-stored payloads, and outbound SSH tunnels.

  • South Korean authorities and four security firms disclosed a state-sponsored campaign that compromised trusted domestic websites to exploit locally installed financial-security software and infect targeted visitors with SIGNBT or COPPERHEDGE backdoors.
  • KISA said AnySign4PC versions 1.1.4.4 through 1.1.4.6 are affected by a buffer overflow that permits remote code execution and lists version 1.1.5.0 as the fixed release.
  • AhnLab said it found evidence of related attacks at 72 organizations in 2026 and identified 15 legitimate websites used as watering holes.
  • AhnLab reported overlap between the state-sponsored activity and Gunra ransomware intrusions, including the same initial-access vulnerability, malware filenames and execution patterns, SSH key fingerprint, and network infrastructure, but said this does not prove the same actor conducted both operations.
  • The reports recommend hunting for suspicious DLL loading by legitimate executables, encrypted data stored under service-registry entries, in-memory PE execution, unusual service creation, injection into SyncHost.exe or svchost.exe, and unexpected outbound SSH tunnels.

Silver Fox targeted a Japanese industrial manufacturer with a phishing-led attack chain that uses DLL sideloading and a modular three-driver BYOVD framework to disable security controls and deploy ValleyRAT. The campaign shows the group is improving resilience with driver-swapping capability, NTDLL unhooking, process injection, and dual watchdog recovery mechanisms to keep the implant running.

  • Silver Fox targeted a Japanese organization in the industrial manufacturing sector with an invoice-themed phishing lure that ultimately delivered ValleyRAT, also known as Winos 4.0.
  • The attack chain used attacker-controlled content hosted on legitimate QQ and Tencent Cloud services, a ZIP archive, and DLL side-loading to deploy next-stage components.
  • The campaign used a three-driver bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver framework involving BootRepair.sys, EnPortv.sys, and wsftprm.sys to gain kernel access and impair security controls.
  • The malware also used NTDLL unhooking, process injection, registry-based payload storage, and two recovery mechanisms to maintain execution.

Kaspersky identified two new heavily obfuscated, victim-tailored backdoors, OctLurk and SilkLurk, used in cyber-espionage against government and related organizations across Central Asia and nearby regions since January 2025. The likely Chinese-speaking actor uses in-memory plugins, proxying, credential theft, remote access tools, and PlugX to maintain access, move laterally, and steal data.

  • The researchers assess with medium confidence that the same Chinese-speaking threat actor operates both SilkLurk and OctLurk, but they could not attribute the activity to any known group at publication time.

Emerging Threat: (CVE-2026-6949) Samba DNS Server Crash via TSIG Name Compression — Should Read

CVE-2026-6949 is a high-severity pre-auth flaw in Samba’s internal AD DNS server that lets a single crafted TSIG DNS packet crash the service, disrupting domain DNS and logons. Affected Samba domain controllers should be patched to the latest fixed releases and have DNS exposure restricted to trusted networks.

  • CVE-2026-6949 is an out-of-bounds write in the internal DNS server included with Samba’s Active Directory Domain Controller, triggered by a DNS packet whose TSIG record uses DNS name compression.
  • The vulnerability is reachable over the network before authentication, requires no privileges or user interaction, and a single crafted packet can crash the Samba DNS process.
  • Every Samba version since 4.0 is affected when used as an Active Directory Domain Controller with the internal DNS server, while Samba deployments using BIND9 through the DLZ module are not affected.
  • The Samba Team released fixes in versions 4.24.5, 4.23.10, and 4.22.11 on July 28, 2026, and Ubuntu, Debian, and Slackware also published fixed packages or advisories.
  • Recommended actions include identifying Samba domain controllers using the internal DNS server, restricting UDP/53 and TCP/53 to trusted networks, reviewing public DNS exposure, and monitoring for DNS process crashes or restart loops.

Cyber extortion group ExfilSquad claims it stole data from two UK Department for Education portals and is demanding a ransom, though officials say the exposed information is limited to customer service contact details and the risk to individuals is low. Microsoft Copilot for Word Can Copy Hidden Prompts Into New Documents — Should Read

A researcher showed that hidden prompt-injection text in Word documents can make Microsoft 365 Copilot alter report data and copy the same concealed instructions into new documents, allowing the manipulation to persist across later Copilot drafting sessions. Microsoft applied mitigations, but the researcher says the broader attack class remains exploitable and requires users to treat external or Copilot-generated documents as untrusted.

Interactive Brokers W-8BEN Lure Hid Behind a 0-Day Domain — Should Read

A phishing email impersonating Interactive Brokers used a same-day registered domain hidden behind a Cloudflare challenge to evade automated link scanning while attempting to harvest W-8BEN tax and account credentials. The key lesson is that “clean” link-wrapper results are not enough when the final destination is a brand-new, inspection-resistant domain with mismatched sender infrastructure.

  • The final destination domain, ehdgmsrd[.]com, was registered on the same day the email was sent and returned a Cloudflare challenge page to automated scanners.
  • The message reached employees at a U.S. healthcare provider, including an occupational therapist and three colleagues, despite having no account-specific identifiers beyond the recipient address.
  • The sender displayed “Interactive Brokers,” but the actual sending address was login@jlrimes[.]com and the call-to-action led to a separate non-Interactive Brokers domain.
  • The recipient organization’s EdgePilot link-protection wrapper reported the link clean because its proxy loaded successfully, not because the final destination was verified as benign.

Building secure Uniswap v4 hooks — Optional

Uniswap v4 hooks shift key security responsibilities to application developers, and incidents like Cork and Bunni show that weak hook authorization, pool validation, and custom accounting can cause major losses even when the core PoolManager works correctly. Builders should treat hooks as high-risk custom logic and rigorously validate callers, pools, deltas, permissions, external dependencies, and callback state.

  • Uniswap v4 hooks let developers add custom behavior to pools, but this flexibility moves some security responsibilities into application and hook code.
  • The Cork and Bunni exploits caused more than $20 million in losses and arose from application-specific authorization and accounting logic around hooks, not from flaws in the Uniswap v4 core protocol or PoolManager.
  • Hook developers must validate who can call privileged paths, which pools are legitimate, how custom balances and deltas are accounted for, and whether external integrations can fail or reenter safely.
  • The article identifies recurring hook failure patterns including missing caller checks, trusting user-supplied pool keys, accounting bugs that still satisfy PoolManager settlement, incorrect callback timing, permission-bit mismatches, blocking hook failures, and unsafe callback state changes.
  • The article recommends that builders and auditors use checks such as gating callbacks, allowlisting pools, separating LP funds, fees, and incentives, verifying address permissions, fuzzing adversarial cases, and isolating callback state.

Check Point announced an AI Network Firewall that aims to make existing firewalls intent-aware so they can inspect prompts, model calls, file uploads, API activity, and AI agent behavior in real time.   • The article argues that the network is becoming the control plane for AI security as enterprises adopt AI across employees, applications, autonomous agents, clouds, branches, and data centers.
